stem: A client with advanced cancer receiving active antineoplastic treatment has persistent pain, nausea, and anxiety. The client says, 'I thought palliative care was only for when cancer treatment stops.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Palliative care can be added now to address symptoms and quality-of-life concerns while your cancer treatment continues.
options.B: Palliative care should begin only after the oncology team determines that no further disease-directed treatment will be given.
options.C: Palliative care is appropriate only during the last days of life, so symptom management should remain entirely within routine oncology visits for now.
options.D: Starting palliative care means the treatment goal automatically changes to hospice care and all antineoplastic therapy must be discontinued.

rationale: ASCO's 2024 guideline recommends early referral of patients with advanced solid tumors and hematologic malignancies to specialized interdisciplinary palliative care teams alongside active cancer treatment, particularly when physical, psychosocial, or spiritual distress or quality-of-life concerns are not adequately addressed. NCI likewise states that palliative care may be provided at any point during cancer care and can occur while cancer treatment continues. Palliative care is therefore not synonymous with hospice or an automatic decision to stop antineoplastic therapy.
educational_objective: Explain that palliative care can be integrated early and concurrently with active cancer treatment to address symptom burden, distress, and quality-of-life needs rather than being reserved only for end-of-life care.
source_organization: American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO); National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Palliative Care for Patients With Cancer: ASCO Guideline Update; Palliative Care in Cancer
source_version_date: ASCO guideline published 2024-07 (online 2024-05-15); NCI current fact sheet accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: ASCO 2024 guideline recommendations: early interdisciplinary palliative care alongside active treatment and referral for unaddressed physical/psychosocial/spiritual distress; NCI Palliative Care in Cancer — 'When is palliative care used in cancer care?'
source_claim_supported: ASCO recommends early specialist palliative care for patients with advanced cancer alongside active treatment, especially when symptom or quality-of-life needs are present. NCI states that palliative care may be provided at any point in cancer care and patients may continue cancer treatment while receiving it.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care — interdisciplinary referrals, continuity/coordination of care, client-centered goals, and resource utilization
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — early interdisciplinary palliative-care referral concurrent with active oncology treatment
correction_summary: Rebuilt the original evidence-summary item into a client-centered referral and teaching scenario. Removed the secondary claim that early palliative care may improve survival because it is not required to establish the current nursing decision. Anchored the final item to the 2024 ASCO guideline and NCI guidance showing that palliative care can begin early, address uncontrolled symptoms and quality-of-life concerns, and occur concurrently with active cancer therapy without automatically implying hospice.
audit_findings: Original item summarized broad outcome evidence and included a survival claim that was unnecessary for the tested nursing decision.

The current 2024 ASCO guideline directly supports early specialist palliative-care referral alongside active cancer treatment for advanced cancer, particularly when symptoms or quality-of-life concerns are present.
NCI directly confirms that palliative care may occur throughout cancer care while disease-directed treatment continues.
The rebuilt distractors target the common but incorrect conflation of palliative care with hospice or mandatory cessation of antineoplastic therapy.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported survival promise, or unresolved source conflict.
